Furthermore, we observed a relatively high frequency of spirals with a length of 10 to 50 au, with most of them exhibiting a length of 20 to 30 au. Notably, we found a relatively low frequency of spirals with a length greater than 100 au based on the ALMA observations at 1.3 mm band, which is in contrast to the higher frequency observed in the near-infrared and submillimeter observations at shorter wavelengths.

A recent study of the BigApple force, a non-local three-nucleon force, has been extended to finite nuclei through the Gogny approach in many-body physics. By incorporating the BigApple force into the Skyrme interaction, an energy component of approximately 1-3 MeV was found for specific astrophysical objects, including $\alpha$-cluster nuclei and neutron stars. Notably, the BigApple force was shown to be consistent with or surpasses existing analyses of three-nucleon forces within neutron stars. To further investigate its effects, the BigApple force was divided into three components based on its response to different density environments. These components were then applied to various objects, from light $\alpha$-cluster nuclei to massive neutron stars.

In quantum computing based on trapped ions, the M{\o}lmer-S{\o}rensen gate is an essential operation that relies on the interference of motional states and is made dependent on the frequency of a laser beam used for its implementation. This study addresses the challenge of creating a frequency-robust M{\o}lmer-S{\o}rensen gate by utilizing multiple motional modes that share a same coupling strength with a common set of lasers. Our findings demonstrate that a M{\o}lmer-S{\o}rensen gate can be made frequency-independent when multiple modes with symmetrical coupling to the same lasers are employed. Furthermore, we have found that using three motional modes can significantly improve the gate's robustness against frequency variations. Our proposed scheme for a frequency-robust M{\o}lmer-S{\o}rensen gate using three motional modes can be implemented using the available technology and offers a high level of robustness against various errors.

A class of materials called strongly correlated Dirac materials holds great promise for advanced electronics due to their high speed and low power consumption. These materials feature a unique "Dirac point" in their energy spectrum, resulting in exceptionally fast and efficient information processing. However, the theoretical framework for strongly correlated Dirac materials has been limited to second-order quantum corrections, hindering a precise understanding of how charge spontaneously arranges itself in these materials. Building on this foundation, we have developed a more comprehensive theoretical framework that incorporates higher-order quantum corrections and higher-dimensional generalizations of strongly correlated Dirac materials. This generalized framework enables the prediction of new materials with a specific electronic configuration, where high-energy "band gaps" meet high-speed "Dirac points." These predictions focus on three-dimensional materials and suggest that perovskite-related compounds, specifically Sr$_{1-x}$K$_x$OsO$_3$ with some degree of charge disorder, could exhibit this unique property.

Researchers are exploring the NA62's sensitivity to heavy neutral leptons at the Kamland neutrino sensitivity level. By analyzing $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$ decays, they found that with 2.5 $10^{32}$ $K^+$ decays, the NA62 experiment can achieve a neutrino mass sensitivity of 70 MeV for $m_N < 84$ MeV and 360 MeV for $m_N > 84$ MeV. For the heavy neutral lepton mixing parameter, they estimate the NA62's reach at 0.36 $10^{-7}$ for $m_N < 84$ MeV and 0.26 $10^{-7}$ for $m_N > 84$ MeV. This indicates the NA62 can either surpass or be on par with the Kamland sensitivity with standard beam conditions. Upgrading to pulsed beam conditions will significantly improve detection and allow the NA62 to probe $N\to e\gamma$ decays within the Kamland's discovery reach.

Recent advancements in neural sequence generation have led to the decline in popularity of $n$-gram language models. We investigated previous studies and found that several experiments featuring neural models in conjunction with $n$-gram models had achieved better results than standalone $n$-gram models. However, these studies overlooked the potential benefits of $n$-gram models by not utilizing them at their full potential. We posited that $n$-gram models could serve as a pre-trained foundation for neural models. To validate this hypothesis, we conducted a series of experiments using a residual learning framework with a focus on tuning neural models on specific tasks. Our findings revealed that starting from a randomly initialized neural model yielded the best results. We also explored other initialization methods as well as low-cost training regimes. In addition to list-level experiments, we created a general text generation model using a massive corpus. The results showed that this model excelled in multiple text generation tasks when fine-tuned. We open-sourced this model on GitHub, inviting the community to contribute to its development.

Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant challenges due to frequently missing or occluded facial details. To address this issue, we propose an end-to-end, occlusion-robust 3D face reconstruction framework that utilizes a self-alignment mechanism to enhance reconstruction quality, particularly in heavily occluded areas. Leveraging a dual face regression network, this framework automatically identifies regions with missing information and prioritizes reconstruction there. The self-alignment module employs a face-to-face matching technique to determine areas with inconsistencies between the input image and reconstructed faces, effectively localizing occluded sections without relying on additional annotations. We evaluate our approach on the widely used FFaceroc and CelebF datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance in both reconstruction and verification tasks.

In the context of inflationary cosmology, a specific scenario involving the sudden onset of a period of rapid expansion can result in the formation of primordial black holes. This particular scenario can occur when a small region of space is isolated from the overall expansion due to a sudden shift in the cosmological constant. In the $\alpha$-attractor model of inflation, this scenario can arise when the number of $e$-folds during inflation deviates significantly from its expected value. As a result, the statistical properties of perturbations in this model can exhibit a non-linear response to changes in its parameters. In order to assess the impact of these non-linear responses on the formation of black holes, we need to determine the range of parameters for which the perturbative approach to analyzing the $\alpha$-attractor model is valid. We achieve this by comparing the results from a non-linear, numerical solution for the power spectrum of perturbations with those obtained using a perturbative approach. We find that the range of valid parameters varies depending on the specific $\alpha$-attractor model, but generally falls within the range $10^{-3} < f_{\rm res} / f_{\rm NL} < 10^{-2}$ for the models we analyzed. We also find that the range of valid parameters is more narrowly defined for models with a certain symmetry, known as shift symmetry, which places additional constraints on the power spectrum of perturbations. We investigate the structure of the deepest nodes in marked ordered trees, which we define as the highest most left node that has no right sibling. Our main findings concern the number of deepest nodes, denoted as $d_n$, which varies significantly with the number of marked nodes, $n$. We establish $d_n$'s distribution and probability mass function (PMF), revealing that the number of deepest nodes follows a discrete normal distribution with mean $\frac{2n^{3/4}}{\Gamma(1/4)\Gamma(5/4)}\cdot \sqrt{\frac{\Gamma(5/4)}{\Gamma(3/4)}}$ and variance $\frac{3}{4}$ times the square of its mean as $n$ approaches infinity. Additionally, we compute the expected sum of the deepest nodes' labels, the sum of the deepest nodes' heights, and the expected number of deepest nodes as $n$ approaches infinity. Our results for the number of deepest nodes can be viewed as a specific case of a broader distributional family, which may be of interest in its own right.

This investigation examines how accurately conventional OCR software can capture the numerical contents of election ballot tabulation sheets, in addition to exploring possible avenues for enhancing the accuracy of such software in this context. A review of relevant literature is presented in the methods section, followed by a detailed exploration of our findings. Specifically, we assessed the OCR software's ability to accurately capture the numerical contents of sample ballot tabulation sheets under both ideal and less-than-ideal scanning conditions, discovering areas where improvements can be made. Furthermore, we propose a straightforward statistical method to correct the OCR-generated counts, which we demonstrated through statistical testing to be a reliable and accurate approach.

In recent years, large-scale linear models have been widely adopted in various machine learning applications. When these models are applied to time series data with autoregressive characteristics, researchers have observed that they can achieve small-loss solutions with a high degree of overfitting, without suffering a significant decrease in generalization performance when moving from small to large model sizes. In an attempt to explore this phenomenon further, this study focuses on a basic time series linear model and establishes conditions under a fixed sample size framework that guarantee a small increase in loss when moving from the optimal small-model solution to the optimal large-model solution. Furthermore, as the model size increases beyond a certain point, the loss will converge to a minimum edge value, which is directly influenced by the lowest autoregressive order. Notably, this value reflects the time series autoregressive characteristics and provides a quantifiable measure of the generalization performance's boundary in relation to overfitting.

A key aspect of future energy systems is expected to be decentralized energy production and consumption, made possible by advances in technology and declining costs. In this context, self-sufficient buildings with high energy demands, such as offices and data centers, will play a significant role by producing and storing their own energy. To achieve this self-sufficiency, these buildings will rely heavily on thermal energy storage systems, which enable the extension of system operation beyond the periods of high electricity demand. However, investing in these systems comes with significant costs, and there are associated risks, including uncertainty surrounding future electricity prices, heat demand, and storage degradation. This study addresses the self-scheduling problem for these energy storage systems, considering their long lifespan and low levels of wear, and models storage degradation as a risk-averse stochastic optimization problem. A risk-averse approach is applied to manage the uncertainty surrounding future electricity prices and heat demand, using scenario-based stochastic programming. The results of this study indicate that a conservative risk-averse approach leads to increased investment in storage capacity, whereas a more aggressive strategy can yield higher payback periods, and that risk-averse management can reduce the risks associated with storage degradation, especially in the early years of its lifespan.

A simplified computer model is used to study and compare different circulation patterns in a planet's atmosphere by simulating a terrestrial environment with varying rotation speeds. This model, which focuses on atmospheric circulation, can operate across a wide range of rotation speeds and allows for the examination of atmospheric circulation under conditions of very slow and very fast planetary rotation. The study of a slowly rotating planet with a low amount of atmospheric gas results in a state of turbulent circulation, characterized by a slow upper atmospheric wind speed compared to the lower atmospheric winds. This state is similar to the atmospheric circulation observed on Earth.

Deep neural networks have achieved superior performance in various classification tasks with the help of a large amount of labeled data. However, creating such datasets is extremely time-consuming and costly. Active learning addresses this challenge by selecting the most effective data points from a vast, unlabeled pool to label, thereby reducing expenses and saving time. Active learning through the most pivotal data points can be achieved through several methods, including maximum variance, expected error reduction, and representative subset selection. These methods have shown significant performance gains in tasks with limited labeling. In contrast, our study highlights the potential risks of active learning in certain situations, where previously accurate models may experience decreased performance after being trained on a subset of the data. Our research focuses on the massive ImageNet dataset and presents a novel approach to active learning that considers the impact of adding new data points on the model's performance. We demonstrate that this approach yields a more stable and more effective strategy for selecting data points for labeling, resulting in a significant improvement in classification accuracy when labeling a fraction of the ImageNet dataset.

Our research involves creating a simulation framework based on multi-valley effective mass theory to model silicon donor electrons in a Hanle setup, consisting of two spinless donors with a tunnel coupler in close proximity. This framework, utilizing a full configuration interaction approach, simulates the impact of exchange coupling on the Hanle signal. We have specifically investigated exchange coupled donors with a tunnel coupler in a position where the Coulomb blockade is broken, and our results indicate that the Hanle signal's precession frequency can be accurately determined even when the Fermi level is deep within the conduction band. Our findings also reveal that the effective mass model can replicate the experimental results of Koppens et al. for single donors under an applied electric field, with the added benefit of predicting new spectral features associated with the two-valley configuration. With this framework, we have explored the possibility of realizing a quantum logic gate using a coherent tunneling between two spinless donors, and our results suggest that it may be challenging due to the small number of relevant configurations compared to the total number of configurations, although this issue could be mitigated by adjusting the position of the tunnel coupler.

Our investigation focused on the transport properties of HgTe quantum wells near their critical thickness, where the energy gap is minimal and semiconductor-to-semiconductor properties are transformed. By integrating quantum well structures into mesoscopic devices, we studied two types of HgTe-based samples: those with a thick Te layer and those with a thin Te layer. When the Te layer is thick, we found a non-zero resistance at low temperatures, indicating the presence of scattering from interface roughness. However, for the thinner Te layer samples, extremely low resistances were observed at low temperatures, suggesting that interface roughness has a negligible impact. Instead, these samples exhibited high mobilities and resistances that varied with energy, which could be explained by a theoretical model of band structure. Notably, the resistances of the thinner Te layer samples align with those predicted for Dirac electrons in graphene, suggesting that HgTe quantum wells at this thickness also behave as a semiconductor with Dirac electrons.

In Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD), individual cells can schedule uplink and downlink modes independently, depending on local traffic conditions, but this creates a mode-scheduling conflict among neighboring cells. This conflict hinders the effectiveness of Dynamic TDD, a key feature of 5G systems, by limiting their ability to adapt to varying traffic scenarios. To address this challenge, we propose a novel Game-Theoretic approach that enables cells to determine optimal mode schedules for their uplink and downlink transmissions. By formulating a non-cooperative game, we can obtain a Nash Equilibrium (NE), which represents the most desirable mode schedules for each cell in a way that no cell can improve its outcome by unilaterally changing its mode schedule. Simulation results under various traffic conditions demonstrate that our proposed solution yields significant improvements in system performance, including increased throughput and improved user experience, compared to traditional static TDD approaches.

In this work, we introduce a novel meta-learning framework centered on ODE neural networks, which acquires an understanding of gradients. This framework enables efficient optimization on new tasks by leveraging learned gradient information, bypassing the need for adjustable hyperparameters. Through extensive experimentation with several benchmarks, our method demonstrates superior performance when compared to traditional meta-learning approaches.

As artificial intelligence models continue to grow in complexity, ensuring their reliability and safety is a pressing concern, particularly in high-stakes applications. Despite significant advances in machine learning robustness, the possibility of sudden, catastrophic failures under specific inputs poses a persistent challenge. This research addresses this issue by developing a collaborative framework among artificial intelligence agents that aims to enhance the trustworthiness of a machine learning model by identifying and rectifying vulnerabilities. The proposed method employs an automated detection mechanism to pinpoint instances where the model is flawed, after which two types of agents intervene: those that generate targeted data corrections and those that conduct safety checks on the model's predictions. Through online collaboration, the machine learning model updates its knowledge in response to guidance from the correction agents and incorporates a trust score that reflects its confidence in its predictions. This approach results in a significant improvement in the model's accuracy in previously untested data, as demonstrated by a notable decrease in errors and an increase in the diversity of new data with high trust scores.

A newly defined polynomial, referred to as the nth toroidal colored Jones polynomial, is established for links in a thickened torus. This polynomial exhibits numerous properties similar to the colored Jones polynomial, and most notably, demonstrates a relationship with the volume conjecture. Specifically, for a link L in S^3, if the volume conjecture holds for a specific metric, then the nth toroidal colored Jones polynomial of L is conjecturally equal to a certain absolute value of a specific eigenvalue of a particular operator associated with L, raised to a power proportional to the volume of L in that metric.

In Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD), a sentence's context is matched against a word's varying meanings, with the goal of identifying the appropriate sense. Given the complexity and subjectivity of this task, several approaches have been explored, including utilizing neural networks. Our study employs a different method, based on the Context-gloss Augmentation (CGA) technique, which involves creating and combining gloss summaries with augmented context. We generate these summaries by replacing words in a sentence with a word's definition, and then selecting the most descriptive phrases. Our proposed framework incorporates CGA via a voting system, with the aim of improving the performance of a pre-trained BERT model. To support this approach, we gathered a large-scale WSD dataset, consisting of over 10,000 annotated sentences. Our results show that CGA-based methods outperform traditional approaches to WSD, with a notable improvement in the F-score on the SemEval 2017 Task 13.

This study develops a genuine integral expression of Riemann's Gamma function in terms of a modified hypersingular integral. We achieve this by translating an analogous complex representation of the Gamma function, initially derived using the Inverse Mellin transform and a modified Hankel transform of a specific distribution, into an integral form using a change of variables. We also establish a connection between the regularized Gamma function and a specific distribution by employing the Mellin transform, in addition to examining the convergence of the developed integral representation through the use of an analytic continuation approach.

The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks for the first time using proton-lead data at an 8.16 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy. Top quark production was identified in events featuring one isolated electron or muon and four or more jets, from a data set totaling 174 inverse nanobarns of luminosity. The measured signal exceeded the five-standard-deviation threshold expected for a background-only hypothesis, and the cross-sectional measurement for top quark pairs was found to be 45 nanobarns with an 8-nanobarn uncertainty, consistent with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics.

This study focuses on key aspects of cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing, specifically schema linking and value filling. We develop a novel end-to-end approach that combines two decoding phases to tackle these challenges. Initially, a unified SQL code is produced through standard decoding. This code serves as a foundation for refining the schema linking and filling values in a second phase of decoding. We postulate that this two-stage approach enables the model to focus on difficult tasks like schema linking during the secondary phase. To evaluate this hypothesis, we introduced a new evaluation metric, F1-None, which disregards the influence of pre-specified schema links. Our experiments on the Spider dataset reveal that the proposed approach excels in both categories, with an improvement of 2.13 in F1-None and 1.33 in execution success. To ensure fairness in comparison, we also explored a large language model for task augmentation but found it to be less effective.

This paper delves into the utilization of differential privacy in the context of graph-based data, which has seen a significant surge in applications and methodologies but struggles with computational complexity. Despite this, researchers have successfully adapted differential privacy to various graph-related tasks, including clustering, node ranking, and community detection. These studies have been applied across diverse domains including social networks, genetic data, and recommendation systems. This paper provides an in-depth examination of four key mechanisms for maintaining differential privacy on graph-based data: perturbation-based mechanisms for publishing graphs, private algorithms for graph machine learning, asynchronous mechanisms for massive datasets, and mechanisms for temporal and multi-layered graphs. It also explores the various challenges and potential solutions in three areas: privacy-preserving graph neural networks, private community detection, and social network analysis.

The vast amount of images, data, and resources that Euclid will generate positions the consortium to create comprehensive legacy databases of outstanding quality, encompassing high-resolution near-infrared spectroscopy with significant implications for the study of distant galaxies. These proceedings outline the promising opportunities and scientific breakthroughs Euclid will achieve in the areas of optical and near-infrared photometry, combining data with other prominent sky surveys, employing advanced spectroscopic techniques to analyze the most remote celestial objects, and conducting in-depth analyses of various cosmic components.

Researchers have successfully used hydrodynamic theories to simulate complex dynamics of quantum many-body systems, and this approach has been particularly effective in modeling the behavior of Bose gases in their equilibrium state. A new hydrodynamic method, Phase-Space Stochastic Hydrodynamics, has been developed to simulate interacting Bose gases through hydrodynamics, and this approach can accurately capture non-equilibrium dynamics and two-body interactions. By directly simulating hydrodynamics with stochastic phase-space equations, this method bypasses the need for a specific hydrodynamic formulation and eliminates the requirement for a precise knowledge of viscosity coefficients. Leveraging this method, our simulations have demonstrated the recovery of collisional dynamics in BEC and degenerate Bose gas systems, and have shown that this approach can be applied to a wide range of interaction strengths and temperatures. This novel Phase-Space Stochastic Hydrodynamics framework offers a versatile and efficient tool for modeling the interactions within Bose gases, and can be applied to various experimental scenarios, such as atomic interferometry, BEC collisions, and laser-cooled atomic gases, among others.

Given an independent and identically distributed sequence of letters broken into words based on independent and identically distributed lengths, Aitchison and Gay have established that the empirical process of the words converges to a point process whose characteristic functional is given by the grand canonical negative log-measure, resulting in the words drawn from an infinite population according to that measure when conditioned on a finite population size. This extends the large deviation principle initially established by Eichelsberger for finite populations.

We establish the existence of a minimum surface within a metric space that connects two given points and fits into a specified homotopy class, provided the space contains a surface that connects two points within the homotopy class and has a boundary of positive length.

Recent studies on the 64Ni nucleus using the (Be9, d16Ne9) reaction found several 0+ and 2+ excited states below 4.5 MeV. Previous knowledge about 64Ni included only two 0+ states: the ground state and a 0+2 state at 1477.64 keV. The new data allowed for a 0+2, 0+3, 0+4 classification and revealed that the energy gap between the ground state and the 0+2 state is larger than previously thought. The B(E2; 0+2 → 0+1) and B(E2; 2+1 → 0+1) transition probabilities were also determined and compared to neighboring nuclei. The shape-coexisting 0+2, 2+1 states in 64Ni were found to exhibit a large overlap with the same states in 62Ni, suggesting that the driving force behind their formation is not simply the neutron pair addition but rather a more complex shell configuration. The spectroscopic characteristics of the 0+2 and 2+1 states were studied using a quadrupole tensor interaction within the TDA framework, which successfully explained the large B(E2; 2+1 → 0+1) probability and the energy difference between the 0+2 and 2+1 states.

Machine learning models often employ k-fold cross-validation (CV) to estimate model performance during parameter tuning. While k-fold CV is beneficial for obtaining an unbiased estimate of a model's expected performance, it is known to increase the variance of this estimate. Consequently, a smaller k is typically chosen to minimize this variance, albeit at the expense of introducing bias into the estimate. Unfortunately, the optimal k for a given problem is often difficult to determine, and our results suggest that a more effective approach may be to use j-k fold CV. In this variant, the inner CV loop has a smaller k than the outer loop. Our experiments using English language models on the SQuAD dataset demonstrate that j-k fold CV can significantly reduce variance while producing similar results to k-fold CV for a range of k values. Moreover, we found that j-k fold CV is particularly beneficial when the number of training examples is limited. Our code is available at https://github.com/nyk157/jk-fold-CV.

Deep neural networks have achieved significant breakthroughs in various tasks due to the massive amounts of data they can process, despite requiring substantial training data. However, numerous critical applications, including those involving limited data, impose a stringent requirement on model size, leading to the development of knowledge distillation techniques. Among these methods, the teacher-student architecture has proven highly effective, with a large 'teacher' model sharing its knowledge with a smaller, more efficient'student' model. As a result of its widespread adoption, the community has a pressing need to synthesize existing knowledge on this approach. This survey delves into the theoretical foundations of teacher-student models, exploring their applications across multiple domains, before examining several key aspects, including optimization strategies, evaluation metrics, and code sharing. Furthermore, the survey concludes with an examination of the numerous open issues and potential future directions in this field of research.

We introduce a new efficient representation called Variable Elimination Preprocessing (VEPP), which leverages function representation and concise Boolean function compilation. Our approach combines these methods to create a compact representation that accelerates the computation of exact Most Probable Explanation (MPE) and constrained optimisation through variable elimination. Our experiments using the MPE and Constrained Optimisation task from the 2019 WASSA challenge showed a 4-fold speedup over existing state-of-the-art implementations. Furthermore, we achieved a 2-fold speedup over the same baseline on real-world graphical models.

We investigated the absorption of a single, monochromatic light beam at 689 nm as it passes through a cloud of ultracold $^{88}$Sr atoms. Due to the interaction, the absorption pattern deviates from a standard Airy pattern because the loss of photons affects their own distribution. To accurately describe this interplay, we employed a stochastic version of the linear system's response. Our findings were also in line with an analytical approach that accounted for the impact of photon recoil, even though this typically has a minimal effect given the large number of interacting photons. Our research utilized a light beam that was nearly two orders of magnitude more intense than previous similar studies.

When subjected to high stresses, certain complex fluids exhibit a sudden and dramatic shift from fluid-like behavior to rigid, solid-like behavior, a phenomenon known as shear thickening. Despite its intriguing nature, the underlying mechanics of shear thickening remains poorly understood. Our study involves creating a comprehensive database of stress versus strain rate data for a polymer-based suspension of rigid particles and reveals that, in a specific range of high shear rates, the relationship can be accurately described using a single, universal scaling formula that captures the essence of shear thickening. By applying this scaling, we gain insight into the specific shear thickening transition and also find that the same scaling formula applies to a broader range of materials and shear rates, effectively grouping them into distinct categories based on differences in their scaled forms. Our findings are supported by both statistical analysis and direct comparison, and we propose that this universal scaling may serve as a fundamental indicator for classifying materials and predicting the shear thickening transition in a wide range of complex fluids.

We establish a connection between the $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ loop algebra and a variant of the Racah algebra, leading to the derivation of the $Z$-series for the $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ loop algebra via its underlying root system. Furthermore, this approach enables a transformation of the Hilbert-Poincar\'e series of the centralizer $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ into a specific G\"unther series, which can be recognized as equivalent to the Apery series.

A well-structured and effective web search engine relies heavily on web search personalization to filter out irrelevant information based on past queries and browsing history. However, this same personalization can lead to web search failures when they result in missed relevant information. To better comprehend the extent of this issue, we conducted two identical searches for lists of web pages using Google's Custom Search, but with one search being influenced by web search history. The difference in search outcomes was then assessed in a series of user studies, where participants were presented with the two different sets of search results for the same query. The studies revealed that even with web search history enabled, many users failed to identify the more comprehensive search results, and that the extent of missed relevant information varied widely, sometimes being quite substantial. These findings underscore the importance for organizations to be aware of web search failures and their potential consequences, and highlight the need for alternative information discovery approaches that can supplement web search.

A new muon-proton or muon-nucleus collider in the 0.5 TeV to 2 TeV energy range is proposed for the site of the Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory (FNAL). This facility, which would require a $6 billion investment, is poised to advance our understanding of quantum chromodynamics by studying high-energy collisions involving muons rather than electrons or photons. By minimizing interference from electromagnetic forces, this collider can delve deeper into the inner workings of strong force than a comparable hadron collider. With the capacity to provide accurate measurements of structure functions in muon-nucleus collisions and offer precise determinations of the nucleon's light quark distribution, it would significantly enhance our knowledge of the fundamental components of matter.

A novel approach has been proposed for imaging the respiratory cycle across the body using MRI, incorporating compensation for organ-specific movement. This method combines three techniques: variable TR time-shifting, golden-angle Cartesian sampling, and a multi-shot turbo spin-echo sequence, within a single sequence. This sequence enables the simultaneous acquisition of respiratory information and high-quality 3D images in just one scan, without the need for retrospective reconstruction methods. This novel sequence has been applied to the abdomen and thorax, yielding detailed 4D images with accurate registration, and has been compared to a conventional stop-and-go method using free-breathing data. This new sequence has been found to provide comparable image quality while reducing scan time by approximately 50%. This sequence has the potential to be a valuable addition to clinical protocols, offering improved patient comfort and faster imaging, and its design is highly adaptable for use with other MRI sequences.

The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has seen significant improvements, enabling the use of high-resolution tests at a low cost. However, the increase in exact paired-permutation testing costs has led some systems to switch to approximate methods for higher-resolution tests. To address this, a new paired-permutation testing library is proposed that utilizes a novel testing framework based on structured test statistics. By leveraging this framework, the library optimizes exact paired-permutation testing for various common tests, including the Watson test and the modified Kendall's W test. Evaluations across three NLP tasks demonstrate that this library matches the speed of approximate paired-permutation testing while maintaining the accuracy of exact methods.

A comprehensive dataset of freight rates, shipping quantities, new ship prices, used ship prices, and scrapped ship prices has been assembled from 1966 to 2009 for the six primary shipping routes. This dataset, which includes 160 time series variables, has been combined into 24 variables for five distinct shipping categories. The dataset has been utilized to conduct a variety of analyses, including testing for long memory properties in freight rate returns, estimating an autoregressive distributed lag model to analyze the relationship between freight rates and shipping quantities, and examining the cointegrative relationships among new ship prices, used ship prices, and scrapped ship prices.

We define loom spaces as a generalization of veering spaces, incorporating a direction vector. Our primary goal is to demonstrate how loom spaces give rise to veering triangulations. By employing a vector field derived from loom spaces, we establish a one-to-one correspondence with Veering triangulations based on a specific classification. This approach extends the Veering's previous method of obtaining triangulations via a 2-dimensional subdivision of the loom space.

The recent emergence of interest in deep learning models for stock price forecasts is a significant trend, and our research contributes to this movement by presenting a novel hybrid approach. By integrating BERT with GAN, we developed a new model called BGRF for predicting Apple stock prices from 2010 to 2020. BGRF leverages BERT's linguistic capabilities to generate input features and employs a GAN to construct a regression model for output, resulting in a new framework with enhanced performance. When evaluated against five benchmark models using RMSE and MAE metrics, the BGRF model demonstrated superior performance, indicating its potential advantages.

This research investigates double Higgs boson production at future electron-positron colliders with high energy, specifically the International Linear Collider, as it relates to Higgs physics and Effective Field Theories. A comprehensive study is conducted through Effective Field Theories, considering Beyond Standard Model Higgs couplings and extending previous studies to Higgs Effective Field Theory with higher-order terms. This is done to assess the TeV $e^+e^-$ Higgs physics reach. Our findings are presented in the form of BSM Higgs coupling sensitivity limits in Effective Field Theories, with comparisons to existing predictions. Notably, we find that double Higgs production at the International Linear Collider exceeds the Standard Model background at an $e^+e^-$ center-of-mass energy of 250 GeV with 1 ab$^{-1}$ of data, with BSM Higgs coupling sensitivity limits reaching the order of 0.1 at the ILC250. This is particularly notable as this exceeds the predicted sensitivity of other processes, such as Higgs production in the $WW$ and $ZZ$ channels, and $Zh$ production with the $Z$ decaying into bottom quarks.

We investigate non-relativistic general relativity using geometric methods from Dirac approach and spinorial holonomy. Our primary objective is to identify a suitable Lagrangian that describes non-relativistic gravity, taking into consideration the effects of a mass term. Building on the principles of geometric gravity, we develop a non-relativistic geometric framework that incorporates a mass parameter. Within this framework, a modified Einstein-Hilbert action can be constructed, and the corresponding Lagrangian is determined for both the geometric and non-relativistic contexts.

We investigated the drag experienced by a long cylindrical solid moving through a layer of granular material, both with and without fluid saturation, across a range of depths. The cylinder's orientation was varied to study its effect on the resulting drag forces. Our experiments with dry granular material revealed that the drag forces depend significantly on the cylinder's orientation, exhibiting a maximum when the cylinder is aligned with its long axis. However, when the cylinder is positioned at a 45-degree angle, the drag forces it experiences are actually greater than those experienced when it is fully inserted into the bed. Our findings also showed that the cylinder's motion can create a depression in the bed's surface, which in turn affects the drag it experiences. When the cylinder is moved through a layer of saturated granular material, it experiences greater drag than in dry conditions, and the anisotropy of drag anisotropy is less pronounced. Our research also involved analyzing the same phenomenon using a discrete element method simulation, which allowed us to better understand the complex interactions between the grains and fluid.

Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we found minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ with decreasing nucleon-nucleon collision number, similar to $v_2/\epsilon_2$. This behavior is consistent with theoretical predictions stemming from relativistic viscous hydrodynamics. Furthermore, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit similar transverse momentum dependencies, which we attributed to the assumed absence of mass splitting within the model.

The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has achieved precise measurements in two areas of rare phenomena: CP violation in the decays of $D^0$ and $D^+$$ mesons and the semileptonic decays of rare $B$ mesons. These events are extremely uncommon and occur through suppressed pathways, making them ideal for detecting signs of new physics. The rare decays in question involve processes like $B \to K \mu \mu$ and $B \to K \gamma$, which the ATLAS experiment has studied in multiple ways, utilizing integrated luminosities of up to $3.0$ $\text{fb}^{-1}$. The research has yielded several notable findings, including the affirmation of the $A_{\text{CP}}$ parameter at $3.7$ $\sigma$ and the establishment of new, more precise benchmarks for $R_{\text{sl}}$ and $R_{\text{se}}$ of $0.43$ $\sigma$ and $0.37$ $\sigma$, respectively.

Numerical models that mimic specific characteristics of complex systems are referred to as structure-preserving discretisations. These models maintain critical properties intact during the numerical solution process. When employed with certain time-stepping methods, models like the Allen-Cahn, Kuramoto, and Lotka-Volterra equations require special care to preserve their symmetry and stability. To maintain the preservation of these models' structures, time-stepping schemes often employ small time steps, which can lead to computationally expensive simulations due to the large number of time steps required for long-term simulations. To address this challenge, this research explores the use of preconditioned Krylov solvers for time-stepping schemes based on finite differences, with a focus on preserving the structure of the underlying model. By employing these solvers, we can significantly reduce the number of iterations needed for each time step, making large-time-step simulations feasible. Our research includes an assessment of the time-stepping schemes and Krylov solvers suitable for various models, as well as an examination of the impact of long-time simulations on the preservation of the underlying model's structure.

Soft-tissue registration is a critical step in image-guided therapy, particularly for minimally invasive procedures that require precise access to internal organs. Traditional methods rely on user-defined parameters and time-consuming simulation testing. These approaches are less than ideal for busy operating rooms where time is of the essence. A new soft-tissue registration technique based on a pre-trained machine learning model is presented here. This model, a biomechanical phantom, is designed to predict soft tissue deformation using limited non-invasive data, specifically MRI. To evaluate this technique, a phantom model was trained using data from a realistic finite element method model of soft tissue biomechanics. The model was then applied to register pre- and intraoperative MRI scans in six patients undergoing spinal surgery. Results showed that the technique met clinical standards for accuracy and speed, outperforming the widely used demons registration algorithm. Furthermore, the technique was found to be robust in the face of incomplete or inaccurate data, a common issue in clinical settings. The code for this project is available on GitHub at https://github.com/SMPL-Registry.

Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. This estimation process is a complex task, particularly when relying on two-dimensional visual data from multiple animated images. To address this challenge, researchers have developed metric learning methods that compare point correspondences across the animated images. However, these methods typically require labeled training data, which can be difficult to obtain in many real-world applications. To overcome this limitation, this study introduces a novel self-supervised learning approach called Adversarial Neighbor Flow (ANF) that leverages point correspondences across the animated images as labels. In ANF, the goal is to distinguish between point correspondences based on their similarity or dissimilarity, defined by their spatial relationship within the animated images. To achieve this, the study employs a generative adversarial network that compares the distribution of point correspondences across the animated images. To evaluate the proposed method, the study conducts extensive experiments using a large and publicly available dataset of animated three-dimensional models. The results demonstrate that ANF outperforms several baseline methods, including self-supervised learning approaches, and provides robust scene flow estimation even when the input images are heavily distorted.

In recent years, AI models based on artificial neural networks (ANNs) have achieved significant success in various classification tasks. However, their practical use is limited due to high computational requirements and extensive memory needed for storage. This issue is particularly pronounced in applications involving low-power embedded systems. In contrast, spiking neural networks (SNNs) function efficiently by leveraging synaptic plasticity and neuronal adaptation, reducing the need for frequent computations. Despite their benefits, training SNNs to achieve high classification accuracy is a complex and time-consuming process. To address this challenge, we developed a novel Random Neural Network (RNN) architecture that delivers superior performance with minimal parameters. This paper presents an expanded version of our previous work, featuring a more comprehensive evaluation of the RNN model across diverse datasets and adhesion levels. Our findings demonstrate that the RNN model achieves comparable classification performance to ANNs at lower adhesion levels, while also exhibiting a significant decrease in energy consumption.

This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of spin-polarized strange quark matter under a strong magnetic field at finite temperature, applying the MIT bag model. A critical aspect is determining the specific condition under which spin-polarized strange quark matter is denser than nuclear matter, as this density variation affects the configuration of spin-polarized strange quark stars. The study examines the impact of temperature and magnetic field strength on the mass-radius relationship of spin-polarized strange quark stars. It also considers the possible quark star masses as well as its critical temperature for various magnetic field strengths.

A perfect matching in a graph is a set of edges such that every vertex is incident to exactly one edge. A perfect 1-factorization of a graph is a set of perfect matchings for which every edge of the graph appears exactly once. We examine the relationship between a graph that has a perfect 1-factorization and properties of its edge-colourings, specifically that it must have a factor of three times an Eulerian component. We then create a new class of cubic graphs, shown to have a perfect 1-factorization if and only if they have a factor of three times an Hamiltonian cycle, and demonstrate this equivalency for individual components before combining them into a larger graph.

This paper introduces a new approach called Timeloops, which generates system call policies for containerized microservices automatically. Inspired by the concept of interval testing, Timeloops leverages temporary, restrictive system call policies to limit the set of system calls allowed for a microservice during a brief testing period. By comparing the expected and observed behavior of a microservice under these policies, the Timeloops framework identifies allowed system calls and generates a policy for production use. This process is repeated with increasingly permissive policies until a satisfactory level of precision is achieved. Our results show that Timeloops can reduce overhead by 30x and achieve a 90% precision rate in just 13 seconds of testing.

This study develops a Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filter using a partially grid-based birth model to manage sensors in a multi-target context. The grid-based birth model focuses on predicting target birth within specific regions, rather than accounting for global target birth. By concentrating prediction efforts on areas with detected targets, this approach enhances efficiency by reducing computational requirements. The efficacy of this method is demonstrated through simulations, showing it outperforms the standard PMBM filter in terms of accuracy and computational demands.

This study examines the null controllability of a population model that includes an interior degenerate diffusion component. By first establishing a new Carleman estimate for the adjoint system in its entirety, and subsequently deriving a relevant observability inequality, we aim to demonstrate the existence of a localized control action capable of driving the population towards extinction within a finite time frame.

The dynamics of soccer games necessitate a well-timed transition from defense to offense, especially in high-stakes situations. A team's decision to attack or defend in such moments can significantly impact the outcome of the game. While research has examined strategies for soccer teams at equilibrium, there's a lack of studies on optimal actions in non-equilibrium situations. This paper develops a deep reinforcement learning model to optimize actions in critical situations, with the goal of achieving a higher probability of scoring while minimizing the risk of conceding a goal. By training the model using real soccer game data, the results show that it can accurately model a optimal policy of attack or defense given the game's state. When compared to a commonly used random policy and an alternative reinforcement learning model, the deep reinforcement learning approach leads to a higher probability of scoring and a lower probability of conceding a goal in simulated games.

High-resolution subsurface modeling via seismic imaging is highly dependent on accurate waveform inversion. However, traditional full-waveform inversion is impeded by local minima in its optimization problem due to its large-scale and nonlinear nature. This issue has been mitigated in the frequency domain by employing data residual and source encoding methods. We have adapted these strategies for time-domain waveform inversion, initially a less explored area. Although time-domain methods can offer advantages, such as simplified source encoding and better stability, they have seen limited application. This study leverages encoded sources and data residual objectives in time-domain waveform inversion, introducing a new time-domain formulation for an extended source waveform inversion problem. Numerical experiments have shown that this new method can handle large models and provide images of similar quality to those obtained from frequency domain extended source waveform inversion.

To analyze the interplay of species competition and dispersal, an asymmetric noisy voter model was developed for a regular lattice structure. The model allows one species to colonize nearest-neighbor sites, while another species can settle at any distance but is less successful in doing so. The model includes external noise, which can lead to random species swaps in the lattice. The combination of these dynamics results in various species competition outcomes, including the exclusive presence of one species, multiple species coexisting, or periodic patterns of one species dominating the others. The effects of noise on species dynamics were examined and found to depend on dispersal rates. Specifically, in a noisy environment, faster dispersing species can exclude slower dispersing species of similar settlement success, even if they have a higher birth rate. This phenomenon is attributed to the tradeoff between colonization and competition abilities.

This research focuses on an integrated data and energy transmission network, which incorporates D2D communication. This hybrid network enables a source node to transmit data to a destination node and simultaneously transfer energy to another node. This integrated approach can lead to significant gains in both data transmission rates and energy harvesting efficiency. However, this system also faces challenges due to its complex interference, as both D2D communication and energy transfer can create interference in the uplink transmission. To address this, we propose a new scheduling algorithm that minimizes interference and enhances network performance. Additionally, an ISRCN (Intelligent Surface-assisted Radio-Communication Network) architecture with integrated energy harvesting capabilities is introduced. This architecture utilizes an intelligent surface that can direct data transmission signals and redirect unused frequency spectrum for new energy transfer opportunities. This enables the network to adapt to changing environments and optimize performance. This integrated network can also support multiple D2D communication pairs and prioritize data transmission and energy harvesting tasks accordingly. This research presents various performance metrics and conducts extensive simulations to evaluate the proposed scheduling and ISRCN architectures. The results show that both algorithms significantly improve network performance, with the ISRCN architecture achieving notable gains under different scenario configurations.

The growing need to maintain social distancing during measurements in complex environments has led to a desire for conducting 2D velocity measurements remotely using a single-point LDV system. This technique can be applied in various settings, including in research on ocean and river currents, as well as within industrial processes. To achieve high-quality measurements, a static anemometry system was developed and tested, featuring a 2D measurement capability. This system uses two separate LDV systems with their own lasers and photodetectors, which can be operated independently to measure the velocity components in x and y directions. To validate the static anemometry system, it was tested using a flow generated by a grid with known velocity characteristics. The results showed that the system can accurately measure velocities across a range of turbulence levels. To facilitate remote operation, a user interface was created to control the system and display the 2D velocity measurements in a graphical format. This interface enables the operator to adjust the signal threshold, choose from different signal processing methods, and calibrate the system to account for any misalignment. To facilitate easy integration with existing data collection systems, the interface uses standard communication protocols. To test the system's performance under real-world conditions, it was used to measure the 2D velocity profile in a wind tunnel with a turbulent airflow. The results from the 2D measurements were compared to 3D velocity measurements obtained using a stereoscopic LDV system and showed a high level of agreement.

The effectiveness of programmable phase plates in enhancing image resolution in the TEM has been subject to debate, with some studies suggesting they can improve image quality and others indicating a limited impact. This study investigates the capacity of programmable phase plates to correct spherical aberration in the TEM, with a specific focus on the TEM's conditions and design. Using a Monte Carlo simulation, we examined how programmable phase plates interact with electrons at the specimen and in the electron camera, and how this affects their ability to correct spherical aberration. Our findings suggest that programmable phase plates primarily function as optical elements that shape the electron beam, modulating its intensity in response to varying voltage patterns. Consequently, their ability to correct spherical aberration relies on the remaining aberration in the TEM, with values indicating that they may not correct high levels of spherical aberration. Notably, our results also reveal that programmable phase plates can produce images with improved contrast, even without correcting spherical aberration, by modulating the image formation process through the distribution of electron intensity.

We provide conditions for the spectral and orbital stability of solitary waves for a Klein--Gordon equation with an anharmonic oscillator, expanding on the work of Benci and Grasso who initially investigated this scenario for a self-dual harmonic oscillator. Our research focuses on both the anharmonic and anisotropic cases to ensure the desired stability.

We derive new conclusions regarding the additive Galois module properties of specific wildly ramified finite non-abelian extensions of Q. Notably, in cases where K/Q is a Galois extension with a Galois group isomorphic to A4, S4 or A5, we establish that the ring of integers in K is freely generated over its ideal associated with 2 when the ramification index at 2 exceeds 7.

In experiments involving particle collisions, the absence of specific events can provide equally valuable insights to the discovery of new phenomena. This study focuses on utilizing non-observed events resulting from the decay of certain mesons in high-energy collisions to constrain the properties of a theoretical particle called an ALP (axion-like particle). By employing a new statistical approach, we have determined the most precise bounds on the coupling and mass of an ALP as it decays into a photon and a neutrino, based on data from the D0 and LHCb experiments. Furthermore, this study demonstrates the potential of future experiments at the Belle II facility to either detect new particles or establish their non-existence through the most precise limits yet set on their properties.

This study examines the potential of contextualized language models in detecting
semantic change across time, as it manifests in word senses. We conducted a
series of experiments utilizing the Word Sense Change Corpus, a recently
introduced dataset featuring words whose meanings have evolved over time. Our
main objectives were multifaceted. Firstly, we sought to assess the ability
of contextualized language models to accurately identify words with shifting
meanings through a task known as MMR-WS. Secondly, we aimed to evaluate the
performance of these models in pinpointing the periods when such semantic
changes began to occur, represented by the Task SC. Lastly, we explored the
connection between semantic change and various contextualized language model
evaluations by conducting the Task C. Our findings reveal that contextualized
language models excel in detecting words with changing meanings but struggle
to pinpoint the exact time periods when such changes started to occur. We
also discovered a significant correlation between the onset of semantic change
and the peak contextualized language model evaluation scores. Notably, our
results showed that the contextualized language model evaluation scores for
words with shifting meanings tend to peak during the middle periods of our
analysis window, a finding that we attribute to several factors including
the nature of our evaluation window, the characteristics of contextualized
language models, and the dynamics of semantic change itself.

Active galactic nuclei (AGNs) are characterized by the emission of electromagnetic radiation from accretion onto a supermassive black hole at the center of a galaxy. The study of these objects through their electromagnetic spectra reveals a lack of emission in the X-ray band below a certain threshold, which can be attributed to the depletions of mass and angular momentum caused by the extraction of energy and spin by an ultralight boson via a process known as superradiance during the AGN phase. This effect results in the formation of a "gap" in the frequency spectrum of the black hole. The remaining accretion power is then channelled into the emission of the ultralight boson, which can be oscillations of the vacuum, such as the stardard model scalar, vector or fermion fields. In this work, we examine the properties of ultralight bosons based on the spins of heavy quasars, specifically focusing on the masses of axion-like and vector-like scalars, and the masses of Dirac and Majorana fermions. We also investigate the potential role of these ultralight bosons in the evolution of heavy quasars and their surrounding environments.

A distinctive feature of neural development is interkinetic nuclear migration (IKNM), where cell nuclei within the neural plate move between the upper and lower edges of the plate as new neurons are generated. In the developing zebrafish retina, IKNM results in retinal neurosphere formation through the gradual accumulation of neurons at the upper edge. To better understand this process, we analyzed IKNM across multiple retinal sections and over time in live zebrafish embryos. Through 3D image reconstruction and quantitative tracking, we found that IKNM follows a random, three-dimensional diffusion pattern, with slower movement towards the upper edge due to retinal growth. By comparing different retinal levels, we identified a common diffusion coefficient for IKNM, suggesting that varying neuronal birthplace is a key factor in neuronal position in the adult retina. Our findings also suggest that the upper edge's increased thickness in the adult retina could result from a sudden cessation of IKNM towards the end of development, rather than a prolonged period of rapid growth.

In various image processing tasks, including video compressed sensing and color image demosaicing, images must be separated from coded measurements that represent their superposition. Real-world code patterns, which are often non-negative, systematically structured and non-Gaussian, can impede reconstruction performance by failing to adhere to ideal coded measurements. This research addresses this challenge specific to code patterns in image compressed sensing. A novel approach is introduced that utilizes a generalized version of the K-SVD algorithm to create a code-optimized dictionary for reconstruction. This dictionary is specifically designed to reconstruct images from coded measurements that reflect real-world code patterns, even when those patterns are non-uniform and vary across different pixels. Real-world code patterns used in this research include those found in compressed CMOS image sensors and JPEG compressed video.

We've developed a comprehensive hydrodynamic theory that applies to polar active fluids in the presence of randomly distributed inclusions, and our model demonstrates the possibility of overcoming these obstructions to maintain a non-zero overall speed. Contrary to previous assumptions, the dynamics of this specific class of active matter cannot be accurately captured using simplified hydrodynamic models when the spatial environment is two-dimensional up to five-dimensional space; however, we have successfully derived precise hydrodynamic equations that effectively describe these phenomena for $d=2$ to $d=5$ spatial dimensions.

The growth of deep learning in OCR has significantly improved, enabling high-quality OCR on complex documents with varied layouts. This project involves creating an extraction system for Indonesian ID cards using NIK and alamat fields. Initially, an OCR is employed to convert the ID card into text, followed by a series of NLP techniques to extract the desired information from the text. A rule-based approach is utilized to remove errors introduced by the OCR, resulting in an extraction efficiency of 92%. The extracted NIK and alamat fields conform to their respective Indonesian standards, as specified by the Kementerian Komunikasi dan Informatika Republic of Indonesia.

Quantum harmonic oscillators under driving forces have been extensively studied in physics, and their behavior under external driving forces has been broadly classified into three discrete regimes based on the level of dissipation. Researchers have employed a variety of methods to examine these transitions using both analytical and numerical approaches. In our study, we employed a path-integral Monte Carlo simulation to investigate the driven harmonic oscillator in its high-temperature limit and its low-temperature limit in the over-damped regime. This numerical approach allowed us to directly calculate expectation values of physical operators by sampling imaginary time correlations. Our numerical results from the path-integral Monte Carlo simulation were found to be in close agreement with the expected outcomes in both temperature limits, thus validating the method. Furthermore, this approach facilitated the calculation of physical quantities in their imaginary time correlations, which are essential for implementing Monte Carlo switching for thermalization.

The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly affects the rotational states of small asteroids by generating a net torque that results in rotation acceleration, primarily visible in their spin periods. By conducting photometric observations of three asteroids, (10115) 1992 SK, (1685) Toro, and (1620) Geographos, we were able to determine their rotation periods and brightness patterns, and in two cases, we also measured precession rates of their equators. The YORP parameters were calculated from both short-term observations of solar incidence lags and long-term observations of rotation periods. The YORP effect was found to be positive for all three asteroids, consistent with theoretical predictions that it should be generally uniform in direction. The YORP values obtained from solar incidence lags and rotation periods showed a notable discrepancy, possibly caused by errors in our measurements or the influence of other forces affecting their rotation. The YORP effect has been found to be strong enough to explain the observed rotation acceleration of two asteroids within their observed timeframes, and it is expected to continue impacting their rotation states well into the future.

We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action within the surface's interior is highly transitive, cannot be topologically compact when using the compact-open topology's inherited structure.

This paper introduces a new framework for creating computable functions that operate on infinite sequences of characters drawn from a given alphabet. Within this framework, a module is established to calculate transducers that can handle infinite sequences, and a second module is developed to generate a representation of function values from these sequences using the $\omega$-regular expressions. A notable contribution of this research involves demonstrating how a specific type of pushdown automaton can be utilized to effectively synthesize the B\"uchi acceptance condition for $\omega$-regular expressions when input sequences are infinite. A key aspect of this framework is the inclusion of an undecidability proof for the problem of determining whether two given type of pushdown automata are equivalent when operating on infinite sequences.

A neural network with multiple coexisting attractors enables discrete variations in task outputs based on input modifications, which can be interpreted as it exhibiting different behaviors for distinct tasks in a single model. However, most research focuses on training models with at least one set of tasks before introducing a second set whose attractors must coexist with the first, despite this capability's potential benefits for tasks such as rapid model reconfiguration, cognitive flexibility, and memory, among others.

Current approaches to jointly train models for multiple tasks simultaneously are often limited to tasks whose attractors have been previously observed, thereby hindering the scope of their applications.

In this work, we develop a novel approach called "Attractor-Mismatch" training, which enables neural networks to adapt to new attractors beyond those seen during training by introducing a new penalty term that encourages a high level of consistency between the current state and the target state, following a significant disturbance.

When applied to multiple benchmark problems, Attractor-Mismatch training yields notable improvements in performance, enabling the model to switch between tasks efficiently and accurately, as well as the ability to incorporate up to 10 new tasks into an existing set of 10 tasks.

To address scalability issues with Eulerian methods for finding optimal controllers under constraints and worst-case disturbances in variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs formulations, we've developed a second-order successive sweep algorithm for calculating the reachable state space. This approach, which assumes a continuous and smooth Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, enables us to determine the states that can be reached within a given time frame under worst-case conditions and state feedback control.

The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain contentious, suggesting that animacy exists along a spectrum rather than a binary divide. Recent evidence indicates that experts in specific domains, such as athletes, can elicit distinct neural responses within the animacy hierarchy. However, the fundamental structure of this hierarchy has not been thoroughly examined across all stimulus types. In this study, a combination of fMRI and a free-sorting method was employed to investigate the animacy hierarchy's organization using action images featuring both high-profile athletes. The results revealed a non-uniform distribution of these images on the animacy hierarchy, with the most animacy-associated region exhibiting reduced sensitivity. Notably, the hierarchy's structure remained stable when restricting the analysis to only the most animacy-associated region. These findings contribute to a more nuanced understanding of the animacy hierarchy's structure, suggesting that it is neither discrete nor linear, and that future studies examining the hierarchy with expert populations may benefit from a domain-specific approach.

The study proves the nonexistence of Landau-Siegel zeros or confirms quantum unique ergodicity for GL_2 Hecke-Maass newforms at a calculable pace, supported by the broader conclusion that Dirichlet L-function zeros exert a force pushing zeros of all even-degree L-functions off the s=1 axis.

We have adapted the quantum relational Hoare logic originally proposed in (Unruh, POPL 2019) to incorporate "expectations" into preconditions and postconditions, thereby enabling the quantification of pre-/postconditions that reflect the relationship between programs' inputs and outputs when comparing pairs of programs.

The rapid dissemination of contagious diseases can be significantly accelerated by isolated incidents of widespread transmission among small groups of people. These events, known as super-spreader occurrences, have been observed in various settings such as sporting events, music festivals, and flights. A mathematical model has been developed to analyze the impact of these events on epidemic spread rates. It considers a population that can be divided into two distinct groups: one where there is a high chance of close contact, reflecting super-spreader events, and another with a lower chance of close contact. The model's findings reveal that even a brief period of rapid transmission in a small group of people can lead to a substantial increase in the overall infection rate of a population. Furthermore, it has been observed that such events often result in delayed peaks in infection rates, potentially occurring after the initial period of rapid transmission has ended. This can be attributed to delayed infections from contacts made during the super-spreader event. This delayed peak may be misinterpreted as an effect of other factors, such as changes in public behavior or government interventions.

Let's consider a complex topological vector space, denoted as X, along with the collection L(X) of continuous linear operators that act on X. This paper aims to extend the concept of codiskcyclicity, initially developed for a single operator within L(X), to a subset of Aarhus, specifically U_Aarhus, and then define codiskcyclic sets of operators in L(X) that act on the space X. These sets must satisfy certain properties, including being closed under the operation of addition and multiplication by scalars. Our primary goal is to explore the codiskcyclicity of certain subsets of operators within L(X), including those that act surjectively on X and the collection of compact operators, as well as the relationship with the spectrum when X is metrizable.

Quantifying solar vector magnetography via magnetograph measurements remains an estimation task prone to variations. This issue is compounded by changes in instrument characteristics over time and differing recovery methods. As a result, various inversion techniques yield a wide range of B_v estimates for the same physical quantity at a given spatial point, leading to inconsistent and potentially misleading inferences about magnetic properties of the Sun. This study delves into the sources of this estimation uncertainty and associated biases by utilizing data from the Solar Optical Telescope and the Helioseismic and Magnetic Instrument Suite on board the Solar Dynamics Observatory. We discovered that while the two instruments employ similar recovery techniques, they employ distinct flux transformations, which the SDO HMI attributes to differing magnetograph sensitivity levels. We also found that both instruments yield similar B_v estimates when using the same recovery method but with a constant offset, and that the estimation uncertainty primarily stems from the offset rather than the specific recovery method used. We developed a correction method for the offset and demonstrated its effectiveness in producing consistent B_v estimates from both instruments. We also explored the effects of this offset on magnetometric inference and discovered that it can masquerade as spurious magnetic signal in certain frequency ranges. We propose enhancing the accuracy of solar vector magnetography by refining the flux transformation and recovering pre-processed magnetograph signals rather than raw data.

A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier to large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem.

Given any non-erasing free monoid morphism σ and subshift X, its image subshift Y under σ and the associated complexity functions p_X and p_Y exhibit the following relationship: there exist constants c, d, and C, where p_X scales by a factor of at least c times d, while scaling at most C, in the sufficiently large integers n in N. If σ is recognizable and letter-to-letter, then p_Y and p_X grow at similar rates, whereas if σ isn't letter-to-letter, there are instances where p_X isn't proportional to p_Y. As a result, topological entropy h_X isn't necessarily preserved when applying σ to X, indicating that defining topological entropy for free group currents F_N isn't feasible. Nevertheless, we can distinguish currents with or without zero or positive topological entropy.

By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of masked language models in unsupervised settings, focusing on models pre-trained for language translation.
A novel approach, called retrieval augmentation, is proposed to direct models towards more adaptable knowledge by selecting contexts similar to unseen target tasks.
To validate this method, we created two datasets featuring spoken language and a written multimodal scenario, where models were trained on a single task but tested on multiple, previously unseen tasks.
The results showed that both unsupervised retrieval and positive sampling techniques improve cross-task generalization.

Optimizing hyperparameters in a privacy-preserving machine learning model has become increasingly challenging due to the restricted access to sensitive data. This research focuses on solving this problem by presenting a novel, efficient method for hyperparameter tuning within a private machine learning framework using deep learning models. A grid search was employed to identify an ideal subset of hyperparameters to tune, followed by the optimization of those selected parameters using a novel, cost-reduced version of the Bayesian optimization method. The proposed approach was evaluated and showed significant improvements in prediction accuracy and model efficiency when compared to traditional methods of hyperparameter tuning. Additionally, the research highlighted the significance of considering hyperparameter privacy in addition to model privacy.

For a Coxeter system denoted by (W,S), we develop the concept of a boolean complex consisting of involutions within W, mirroring Ragnarsson and Tenner's previous work. This boolean complex is parameterized by a subset of S, specifically those with even cardinality. We then establish a connection between the boolean complex of involutions and the poset of intervals within W, equipped with a natural order induced by the length function.
